claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloys have limited strength and ductility.
Adding Ti, Nb, or Mo to eutectic high-entropy alloys enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Adding the proposed alloying elements can simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
The simultaneous increase in strength and ductility is caused by enhanced solid-solution strengthening.
Interactions involving the added alloying elements produce lattice distortion.
Interactions involving the added alloying elements increase dislocation density.
Yield strength may increase by as much as 20% relative to the alloy without the additional alloying elements.
Elongation at break may increase by as much as 15% relative to the alloy without the additional alloying elements.
The expected improvement applies only over an addition range that does not cause significant precipitation or phase separation.
The appropriate baseline is an as-cast or conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy without the additional alloying elements.
Failure to obtain a significant increase in both strength and ductility would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation of significant precipitation or phase separation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes compositions that produce significant precipitation or phase separation from the hypothesis's domain, whereas the falsification rule treats those out-of-domain microstructures as evidence that falsifies the hypothesis.
